extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent practitioners, law students, and members of the public seeking an overview of Canadian patent law and filing/practice requirements
extracted.subtask_description: High-level summary of the substantive and procedural requirements for obtaining, enforcing, and filing patents in Canada, including patentability criteria, excluded subject-matter, filing rules, and infringement concepts. Useful as an orientation for applicants, counsel, and students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability — three core criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: To be considered patentable, an invention must pass three criteria: novelty — the invention must be new; non-obviousness — it must be inventive; utility — the invention must be useful, i.e., functional and operative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the overarching test for patentability. The page repeatedly treats these three as the fundamental gatekeepers for Canadian patents; later sections expand each criterion into statutory tests and case-law-derived analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (anticipation) — statutory test (s.28.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be novel: not previously described or claimed in a third-party Canadian patent application and not previously publicly disclosed by a third party anywhere in the world. Codified under s.28.2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: s.28.2 bars subject-matter disclosed more than one year before the filing date by the applicant (or via the applicant), and bars earlier public disclosures by others and earlier-filed Canadian patent applications by others. Private undisclosed documents do not count as prior disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty — eight‑pronged anticipation test
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an eight-pronged test to determine whether anticipation occurs in Canada: prior art must (1) give an exact prior description; (2) give directions which will inevitably result in something within the claims; (3) give clear and unmistakable directions; (4) give information equal to that given by the subject patent for practical utility; (5) convey information so a person grappling with the same problem would say 'that gives me what I wish'; (6) give information to a person of ordinary knowledge so he must at once perceive the invention; (7) in absence of explicit directions, teach an 'inevitable result' provable only by experiments; and (8) satisfy all these tests in a single document without making a mosaic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires that a single prior disclosure provide all information necessary to produce the claimed invention without inventive skill. The 'no mosaic' principle — you cannot combine multiple prior documents to find anticipation — is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑obviousness (inventive step) — statutory test (s.28.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter defined by a claim must not have been obvious on the claim date to a person skilled in the art, having regard to prior information as described in s.28.3 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: s.28.3 sets the statutory frame; the page cites case law (Apotex v. Sanofi‑Synthelabo) applying an adapted Windsurfing test (identify person skilled in the art and common general knowledge; identify the inventive concept; identify differences between prior art and inventive concept; ask whether those differences would have been obvious without knowledge of the invention). Use of the 'person skilled in the art' and the four-step Windsurfing/Apotex analysis is central to evaluating inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art / common general knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The evaluation of non-obviousness is made from the perspective of a notional 'person skilled in the art' with the relevant common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying the correct notional skilled person and their common general knowledge is a discrete analytical step in the Windsurfing/Apotex framework; this selection affects the inventive-step analysis and claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (industrial applicability/usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a product to have utility it must perform some useful function; the requirement originates from the definition of invention as a 'new and useful art'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility is generally easy to meet but excludes methods/items that would not be useful. Utility limits the scope of protection; an invention must be functional and operative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject‑matter (what may be patented)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject-matter includes: a product, a composition, a machine, a process, or an improvement on any of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: door lock (product), chemical composition used in lubricants (composition), a machine for making door locks (machine), a method for making door locks (process). The page distinguishes these statutory categories from non‑patentable matters discussed separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject‑matter (what cannot be patented)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some matters cannot be patented, including 'disembodied ideas, concepts or discoveries', scientific principles and abstract theorems, methods of medical treatment or surgery, higher life forms, forms of energy, features of solely intellectual or aesthetic significance, and printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list of prohibited matters differs from other jurisdictions. The page also notes certain plant matters and medical treatments within the body are excluded; diagnoses based on tests may be patentable. The exclusions must be considered when drafting claims to avoid abstract or non‑statutory subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer program / software patentability nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer code by itself is not physical and some types of computer programs are not patentable per se; however, CIPO states a computer program may be patentable if it offers a new and inventive solution to a problem by modifying how the computer works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software may be patentable in Canada if it meets the traditional criteria (new, non-obvious, useful) and directly provides a functional real-world useful result beyond mere algorithmic calculation. Drafting should emphasize technical effect or modification of computer operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement (listed requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency of disclosure is listed among legal requirements relevant to patentability (i.e., the application must disclose enough to allow the invention to be practiced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not expanded in detail on the page, sufficiency/enablement is a recognized requirement — the specification should enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing/publication timing — 18‑month publication and patent term
rubrics_metrics.description: All patent applications (unless withdrawn) are made public 18 months from the earlier of the Canadian filing date (or priority date) or the foreign filing date if conditions are met. Patent term: applications filed on or after 1 October 1989 last to a maximum of 20 years after the patent application was filed (older regime: 17 years after issue for pre‑1989 filings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public disclosure via publication aims to balance public access to technological information with inventor rights. Applicants should consider international effects of publication and term calculation when planning prosecution and commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: First‑to‑file system
rubrics_metrics.description: Canada generally grants patents to the first inventor to file an application (since 1 October 1989), producing a 'race to the patent office'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of first‑to‑file, delayed filing risks losing rights even if you were the first inventor. Early filing strategies, provisional/priority filings, and careful public disclosure planning matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: One‑year grace period for applicant disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors have one year after their first public disclosure of their invention in which to file a Canadian patent application (a 'grace period').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosing the invention prior to filing will jeopardize significant international patent rights and may cause loss of the race to the patent office. Relying on the grace period is a domestic safety valve but has international consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting priority / earlier filing date (Paris Convention/WTO)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subsequently filed Canadian patent application can request priority back to an earlier-filed foreign or domestic patent application (within applicable time-limits) to obtain an earlier 'effective filing date' for overlapping subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes the common 12‑month priority window under the Paris Convention/WTO members; priority can affect novelty and obviousness assessments if properly claimed and supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent infringement — exclusive rights and infringing acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Once patented, exclusive rights are granted to the patent holder (s.42 of the Patent Act). Any interference with the patent holder's 'full enjoyment of the monopoly' can be infringement. Making, constructing, using, or selling a patented invention without permission can constitute infringement. Possession, use in a process, and inducement/procurement may also count as infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess infringement by comparing alleged acts to the patent claims and considering statutory rights. The page emphasizes the broad scope of possible infringing acts (including indirect forms like inducement). Remedies and defences are handled in courts (Federal Court, provincial/territorial courts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity (listed concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: The page lists 'presumption of validity' among patentability-related concepts and legal principles relevant to Canadian patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not elaborated in the body text, presumption of validity generally means a granted patent is presumed valid until proven otherwise; challengers bear the burden to rebut validity in litigation or proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Canada is a party to the PCT. The Canadian Patent Office may act as a Receiving Office for international applications, as an International Searching Authority, and as an International Preliminary Examining Authority. The Office also receives Canadian national phase applications under the PCT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the PCT can streamline international filing and searching. Applicants who are Canadian nationals or residents can file PCT applications designating Canada; national phase entry and use of international search/examination products should be planned as part of global prosecution strategy.
